questions.question: According to the law of demand, when the price of a good rises (ceteris paribus), the quantity demanded will:
options: A. Increase
B. Decrease
C. Remain unchanged
D. First increase then decrease
questions.explanation: The law of demand states an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, holding other factors constant. As price rises, consumers buy less. Option A is the opposite, C ignores the relationship, D is unrealistic.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: At market equilibrium, which of the following is true?
options: A. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
B. Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
C. Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
D. There is a shortage or surplus depending on price
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is where the demand and supply curves intersect, meaning the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. Options A and B describe shortages and surpluses, respectively. D is incorrect because equilibrium clears the market.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: If the government sets a price ceiling below the equilibrium price, the most likely result is:
options: A. A surplus
B. A shortage
C. No change in the market
D. An increase in equilibrium price
questions.explanation: A price ceiling below equilibrium makes the legal price lower than the market-clearing price, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage. A surplus occurs with a price floor, not a ceiling.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: A technological improvement lowers production costs. In a competitive market, this will lead to:
options: A. A decrease in supply, raising price and lowering quantity
B. An increase in supply, lowering price and increasing quantity
C. An increase in demand, raising price and quantity
D. A decrease in demand, lowering price and quantity
questions.explanation: Lower production costs shift the supply curve rightward. At the original price, there is a surplus, pushing price down and quantity up. This is a supply-side change, not a demand shift.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: A price floor is set above the equilibrium price. Which of the following is the direct consequence?
options: A. A shortage of the good
B. A surplus of the good
C. The market remains at equilibrium
D. Demand increases to meet the higher price
questions.explanation: A price floor above equilibrium makes the legal minimum price higher than the market-clearing price, causing quantity supplied to exceed quantity demanded, i.e., a surplus. A shortage occurs with a price ceiling.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: An increase in the price of a complementary good will, ceteris paribus, cause:
options: A. A rightward shift in the demand curve for the good
B. A leftward shift in the demand curve for the good
C. A movement along the demand curve for the good
D. A rightward shift in the supply curve for the good
questions.explanation: Complementary goods are used together. If the complement's price rises, consumers buy less of it, reducing demand for the related good. This shifts the demand curve left, not a movement along the curve.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: If both demand and supply increase, which of the following is definitely true?
options: A. Equilibrium price rises
B. Equilibrium price falls
C. Equilibrium quantity increases
D. Equilibrium quantity decreases
questions.explanation: Both curves shift right, so the new equilibrium quantity is higher. The price change is ambiguous because the demand increase pushes price up while the supply increase pushes it down; the net effect depends on the magnitudes.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: Suppose both demand and supply decrease simultaneously. What is the certain effect on equilibrium price and quantity?
options: A. Price falls, quantity falls
B. Price rises, quantity falls
C. Quantity falls, price is indeterminate
D. Price rises, quantity is indeterminate
questions.explanation: Both curves shift left, so quantity unambiguously decreases. Price depends on the relative size of the shifts: if demand falls more, price falls; if supply falls more, price rises; thus price is indeterminate.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: If the price elasticity of demand for a good is 0.5, a 10% increase in price will cause the quantity demanded to:
options: A. Decrease by 5%
B. Decrease by 20%
C. Increase by 5%
D. Decrease by 10%
questions.explanation: PED = %ΔQd / %ΔP. Given PED = 0.5, a 10% price increase leads to %ΔQd = 0.5 × 10% = 5%. Since price and quantity move inversely, quantity decreases by 5%. B would be PED=2, C has wrong sign, D implies unit elasticity.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: A firm increases the price of its product. If the demand is price elastic, total revenue will:
options: A. Increase
B. Decrease
C. Remain unchanged
D. Increase only if the price rise is small
questions.explanation: When demand is elastic, %ΔQd > %ΔP. A price rise causes a proportionally larger fall in quantity, so total revenue (P × Q) decreases. Option A would be true for inelastic demand. C occurs only with unit elasticity. D is irrelevant.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: The price elasticity of supply of a product is likely to be more elastic in the long run because:
options: A. Firms have more time to adjust production
B. Firms have less time to adjust production
C. The product is perishable
D. There are no close substitutes in production
questions.explanation: In the long run, firms can change all inputs, expand capacity, or enter/leave the market, making supply more responsive to price changes. B describes the short run, leading to inelastic supply. Perishability and lack of substitutes also reduce elasticity.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: A firm knows that the price elasticity of demand for its product is -1.5. If the firm cuts the price by 10%, the percentage change in total revenue is approximately:
options: A. 3.5% increase
B. 5% increase
C. 5% decrease
D. 3.5% decrease
questions.explanation: PED = -1.5, so %ΔQd = -1.5 × (-10%) = +15%. New total revenue = (0.9P) × (1.15Q) = 1.035PQ, a 3.5% increase. Option B ignores the cross term (simple sum: -10%+15%=5%), but exact calculation gives 3.5%. C and D have wrong signs or magnitudes.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: Which of the following will cause a rightward shift in the demand curve for a normal good?
options: A. A decrease in consumers' income
B. An increase in the price of a substitute
C. A decrease in the price of the good itself
D. An increase in the price of a complement
questions.explanation: A higher substitute price makes this good relatively cheaper, so consumers switch to it and demand increases (rightward shift). A: lower income reduces demand for a normal good (leftward shift). C: a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift. D: since complements are consumed together, a higher complement price reduces demand for this good (leftward shift).
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: A price ceiling is imposed below the equilibrium price. Which of the following is NOT a likely consequence?
options: A. A shortage of the good
B. Non-price rationing such as queuing
C. A black market may emerge
D. A surplus of the good
questions.explanation: A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage (quantity demanded > quantity supplied). To allocate scarce goods, non-price rationing and black markets often arise. A surplus is associated with a price floor, not a ceiling.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: Which of the following correctly defines price elasticity of demand?
options: A. Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
B. Change in quantity demanded divided by change in price
C. Percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
D. Change in total revenue divided by change in price
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand measures responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, calculated as %ΔQd / %ΔP. Option B is the slope of the demand curve, not elasticity. C is the inverse (elasticity of price with respect to quantity). D is unrelated to elasticity.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: Which factor would make the price elasticity of demand for a good more elastic?
options: A. The good has many close substitutes
B. The good is a necessity
C. The good has few substitutes
D. The good is a small proportion of the consumer's budget
questions.explanation: Availability of close substitutes makes demand more elastic because consumers can easily switch. Necessities and few substitutes make demand inelastic. A small budget share also tends to make demand inelastic, as consumers are less sensitive to price changes.
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: If the cross elasticity of demand between goods X and Y is -2, then a 5% increase in the price of X will cause the quantity demanded of Y to:
options: A. Decrease by 10%
B. Increase by 10%
C. Decrease by 2.5%
D. Increase by 2.5%
questions.explanation: Cross elasticity of demand = %ΔQd of Y ÷ %ΔP of X. Since cross elasticity is -2 (X and Y are complements), %ΔQd of Y = -2 × 5% = -10%, so the quantity demanded of Y decreases by 10%. B has the wrong sign; C and D have the wrong magnitude (they would follow if the elasticity were -0.5).
questions.subject: econ

questions.question: For a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve, the price elasticity of demand at the midpoint of the curve is:
options: A. Unitary elastic
B. Elastic
C. Inelastic
D. Zero
questions.explanation: On a linear demand curve, slope is constant but elasticity varies. At the midpoint, price and quantity are such that the percentage changes are equal, giving PED = 1 (unitary). Above the midpoint, demand is elastic; below, it is inelastic. Zero occurs at the quantity intercept (where price is zero).
questions.subject: econ
